page: Beyond the Classroom — College Life at JNTU GV
heading: A Different World
text: Leaving Peddamadi for Vizianagaram was the first major turning point in my life. For nearly fifteen years, my world had been bounded by the same quiet village roads, the same school, and the same familiar faces. Engineering changed all of that overnight. I enrolled at JNTU-GV, Vizianagaram, as an Information Technology student. To be completely honest, I had no real idea what Information Technology actually meant. Programming. Algorithms. Software engineering. Artificial Intelligence. They were abstract concepts I had never encountered before. Like most first-year students, my worldview was modest: attend lectures, clear exams, and head back home. I assumed college was simply a four-year bridge to a degree. I couldn't have been more wrong. Programming entered my life at eighteen, starting with C. At first, nothing clicked. Compiler errors felt terrifying, every missing semicolon was a mystery, and practical sessions left me bewildered. I wasn't the student who picked up syntax instantly; I was just trying to survive the learning curve. Yet those confusing first programs slowly became the foundation for everything I engineer today.

page: Beyond the Classroom — College Life at JNTU GV
heading: One Friendship Changed Everything
text: Towards the end of my first year, I met Pravallika. Looking back, that single friendship redirected my entire trajectory. While I was still wrestling with basic syntax, she introduced me to web development and pushed me to build real projects rather than just memorize textbook theory. Together, we decided to tackle something ambitious: building an Amazon clone. We followed a five-hour tutorial line by line—pausing every few seconds, debugging obscure errors, and Googling endlessly until we understood why each function worked. It took us thirteen intense days. What seemed like a modest tutorial back then gave me something infinitely more valuable than code: it gave me confidence. After that first breakthrough, learning became infectious. We moved from web development to machine learning, and eventually to Artificial Intelligence. Soon, our evenings were spent dissecting Large Language Models, computer vision, modern web frameworks, and emerging research papers. Every hackathon, every failed prototype, every internship rejection, and every late-night terminal session quietly pushed us further. Curiosity was no longer just a childhood trait—it was becoming a career.

page: Beyond the Classroom — College Life at JNTU GV
heading: Mentorship & The People I'll Remember
text: One door opened another. Through Pravallika, I was introduced to Professor G. Jaya Suma—a meeting that became another pivotal turning point. She challenged me to look beyond syllabus requirements: to ask deeper questions, to publish research, and to explore advanced technologies most undergraduates never touched. Many of the research papers, internships, and AI platforms I've built exist because a professor chose to believe in a curious student. Sometimes, all it takes is one person giving you an opportunity to prove yourself. When I first arrived on campus, I was a quiet introvert who found starting conversations difficult. Thankfully, college introduced me to people who transformed those four years. My senior Mohan Pradeep mentored me through tricky crossroads, while hostel life introduced me to Das and Saroj—friends who quickly became brothers. Our favorite memories weren't scheduled in calendars. A random evening conversation would spontaneously turn into a midnight ride. A free weekend would turn into an unplanned journey to Araku, Puri, or the Vizag coast. No itinerary, no plan—just shared laughter, freedom, and the simple willingness to say, "Let's go."

page: Where Curiosity Began — Life & Stories
heading: Where Curiosity Began
text: Personal stories, growing up in Peddamadi, childhood curiosity, films, and life outside engineering by Likhith Kumar Mankala. My Life in Five Minutes I wasn't born in a big city surrounded by technology. I was born in a small village called Peddamadi, near the Odisha border in Andhra Pradesh. It's such a small place that, for many years, you couldn't even find it properly on Google Maps. Almost my entire childhood was spent there. From primary school to intermediate, nearly fifteen years of my education happened in the same village. It wasn't a place filled with opportunities or the latest technology, but it gave me something much more valuable—a childhood full of curiosity. My father is an RMP doctor who has spent years travelling between nearby villages, treating patients and helping families with basic medical care. My mother runs a small neighborhood shop, where almost everyone in the village knows her by name. Growing up, I also had my two sisters, who were always incredibly supportive and looked after me, especially when I was busy creating chaos. And yes... I was definitely a handful. I wasn't the quiet kid who sat still. I was always running around, climbing things, asking endless questions, and usually finding new ways to test my parents' patience. Looking back, I'm pretty sure I gave them more headaches than peaceful days.

page: Where Curiosity Began — Life & Stories
heading: Toys never stayed toys
text: Some kids played with toys. I wanted to know how they worked. Whenever I received a remote-control car, a robot, or even a small toy airplane, I would happily play with it for a while. But eventually curiosity always won. I'd take it apart piece by piece, spread all the components across the floor, and try to understand what every gear, motor, and wire actually did. Sometimes I'd even combine pieces from different broken toys to build something completely new. It rarely worked—but that didn't matter. Without realizing it, I was already thinking like an engineer.

page: Where Curiosity Began — Life & Stories
heading: Falling in love with technology
text: Technology fascinated me long before I knew what programming was. My first mobile phone experience wasn't even my own phone. It belonged to my father—a small Celkon keypad phone. I spent hours playing the built-in games and pressing every button just to see what would happen. Later, when 3G internet finally arrived, it felt like magic. The signal in our village wasn't exactly reliable. Whenever I wanted a webpage to load, I'd walk outside, stretch my arm into the air while holding the phone, and hope those tiny network bars would become just strong enough to open a website. Sometimes it worked. Sometimes it didn't. Back then, waiting several minutes for a single webpage felt completely normal. Yet every successful page felt like discovering something new.

page: Where Curiosity Began — Life & Stories
heading: The phone everyone wanted
text: One of my favorite childhood memories happened whenever my uncle visited from Mumbai. He owned our family's very first touchscreen smartphone. For us, it wasn't just a phone—it was the most exciting gadget we'd ever seen. All my cousins would gather around at my grandmother's house, passing the phone from one person to another, carefully taking turns to play games before handing it over to the next person. We laughed, argued over whose turn it was, and somehow managed to spend an entire afternoon with a single phone. Those moments are still some of my happiest childhood memories.

page: Where Curiosity Began — Life & Stories
heading: The first computer
text: The first computer I ever touched wasn't at home. It was at my school. I still remember staring at the monitor, fascinated by how clicking a mouse could make things happen instantly. Everything about computers felt magical. That curiosity only grew stronger over time. Whenever I had free time, I found myself exploring phones, computers, software, or anything electronic I could get my hands on. My teachers noticed that curiosity and encouraged me to keep learning, even when I spent more time experimenting than following the usual path.

page: Where Curiosity Began — Life & Stories
heading: Growing up with changing dreams
text: Like many children, my dream job changed almost every year. Sometimes I wanted to become a doctor like my father. Then I dreamed about becoming an astronaut. Later it was the civil services. Then software engineering. Then medicine again. My childhood was a constant cycle of discovering something new and imagining myself doing it one day. Looking back, none of those dreams were really about the job itself. They all came from the same place: I simply loved learning how things worked.

page: Where Curiosity Began — Life & Stories
heading: A Bigger World Than My Village
text: Outside school, I spent countless hours exploring the digital world. Temple Run • Subway Surfers • Angry Birds • Free Fire. Those games introduced me to technology, but the internet opened an even bigger world. I watched funny videos, explored places I'd never seen before, followed food channels, learned random facts, and slowly became fascinated by how people built things online. As I grew older, movies became another source of inspiration. I loved the Marvel universe, and Christopher Nolan's films completely changed the way I looked at storytelling, imagination, and technology. Looking back now, I realize none of those moments seemed important at the time. A broken toy car. A Celkon phone struggling to load a webpage. Waiting for my uncle to bring a touchscreen phone from Mumbai. The first computer in my school. Countless evenings spent exploring the internet. They all looked like ordinary childhood memories. But together, they quietly shaped the person I would become. They gave me something far more valuable than technical skills. They gave me curiosity. And that curiosity eventually led me beyond my village—to engineering, software, and later, artificial intelligence.

heading: Why I Chose AI
text: Insights on Artificial Intelligence, LLM architectures, Autonomous Agents, and why AI is transforming software engineering by Likhith Kumar Mankala. From building websites to building intelligent systems. There was a time when I thought I'd spend my entire career as a web developer. When I first started learning software development, my world revolved around HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, and Next.js. Every new project made me a little more confident, and every completed website felt like a small achievement. I enjoyed building interfaces, connecting APIs, and watching ideas come to life in the browser. At that point, I believed web development was where my journey would stay.

page: Why I Chose AI — Engineering Philosophy
heading: The Question That Changed Everything
text: Around that time, AI coding tools like v0, Lovable, and similar platforms started appearing. For the first time, I watched complete websites and applications being generated in just a few minutes. My first reaction wasn't excitement. It was uncertainty. "If AI could already build websites this quickly, what would software development look like five years from now? Would writing frontend code alone still be enough?" Instead of ignoring those questions, I decided to understand the technology behind them. That curiosity became the beginning of my AI journey.

page: Why I Chose AI — Engineering Philosophy
heading: Starting From the Fundamentals
text: The biggest challenge was that I had absolutely no idea where to begin. Machine Learning. Neural Networks. Deep Learning. Large Language Models. Everything felt like a completely different world. Rather than jumping directly into AI tools, I decided to start from the fundamentals. I enrolled in Scaler's Machine Learning course covering supervised and unsupervised learning. The course itself lasted around fifteen hours—it took me more than a year to complete. Not because it was difficult, but because I wasn't just watching lectures—I was trying to understand every concept before moving forward. Learning became something I fit around everything else happening in my life.

page: Why I Chose AI — Engineering Philosophy
heading: Learning Never Followed a Straight Path
text: While I was studying Machine Learning, I was also working on internships, building production websites, participating in hackathons, and improving my full-stack development skills. During that period, I worked on projects ranging from university websites to production-ready applications, including platforms for DSNLU, portfolio websites, and several client projects. Some days I was building React components. The next day I was reading about gradient descent. Then deploying APIs. Then debugging production applications. Then returning to machine learning again. Looking back, none of it happened in order. And I think that's how engineering really works. You don't master one topic before starting the next. You learn by constantly moving between them.

page: Why I Chose AI — Engineering Philosophy
heading: Discovering Large Language Models
text: Another turning point came through Professor G. Jaya Suma. She encouraged me to start exploring Large Language Models. Honestly, I wasn't very interested at first. Machine Learning already felt like a huge field, and LLMs looked even more complicated. But once I started experimenting with them, everything changed. I began learning about prompt engineering, embeddings, vector databases, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), inference, fine-tuning, local models, and AI system design. The deeper I went, the more fascinated I became. For the first time, I wasn't just building software—I was building software that could reason, retrieve information, and interact with users in completely new ways.

page: Why I Chose AI — Engineering Philosophy
heading: Going Beyond AI
text: As my interest in AI grew, so did my curiosity about everything surrounding it. With guidance from Joel, I explored technologies that supported modern AI systems—from Three.js and CesiumJS to browser automation, GPU optimization, navigation systems, local inference, and developer tooling. I wasn't interested in learning a single framework. I wanted to understand the entire ecosystem: how models run, how agents communicate, how applications scale, and how intelligent software is actually built. That mindset pushed me far beyond tutorials and into building complete systems.

page: Why I Chose AI — Engineering Philosophy
heading: Building My Own Tools
text: Over time, something unexpected happened. Whenever I needed a tool, I stopped searching for one—I started building it. A document workspace became Serea. A repetitive task became an automation. A YouTube downloader became a weekend project. Personal AI assistants replaced manual workflows. Cron jobs handled repetitive work. Small utilities slowly grew into products I used every day. Instead of depending on dozens of separate applications, I found myself creating software designed specifically for the way I work. That completely changed my perspective. Today, I don't build projects simply to learn a technology—I build tools because I genuinely want to use them.

page: Why I Chose AI — Engineering Philosophy
heading: Looking Back
text: Looking back, I don't think I chose AI because it was the next trend. I chose it because it challenged the way I thought about software. Web development taught me how to build applications. Artificial Intelligence taught me how to build systems that can learn, assist, and adapt. Today, my work combines both worlds. I still enjoy designing great software and full-stack development, but what excites me most is building intelligent products that solve real problems. And I have a feeling that this is only the beginning.
